title: How To Cold Email Investors - Michael Seibel
summary: A recipient’s guide to investor emails: explain the business, stage and evidence plainly, keep the first exchange easy to answer, and earn a conversation before demanding a meeting.
notes: Investor-specific advice recorded in 2019; his open-tracking suggestion is historical advice, not a promise that present-day open data is reliable.

title: How To Convert Customers With Cold Emails | Startup School
summary: A full YC lesson covering targeting, one clear outcome, human language, specific personalization, credibility and calls to action. Epstein critiques actual anonymized emails from his inbox, including examples that miss the recipient’s business entirely.
notes: Customer acquisition, recruiting and partnerships—not just fundraising. Example conversion rates and outcome claims are the speaker’s, not independently validated benchmarks.

title: Why You're Getting Zero Replies To Your Cold Emails
summary: Learn manually before automating, identify people who actually own the problem, make the benefit easy to understand, and use language learned from customers. Includes a concrete startup email teardown.
notes: Speaker identified from publisher metadata as YC visiting partner and OneSchema cofounder. The recommended outreach quantities are contextual advice, not universal thresholds.

title: The Perfect Cold Email (according to David Sacks, Keith Rabois, & Jason Lemkin)
speakers: Jason Lemkin, interviewed by Harry Stebbings
summary: Lemkin describes his preference for detailed, evidence-rich pitches and contrasts it with other investors’ preferences. He also recounts missing monday.com because its initial email did not communicate the opportunity.
notes: David Sacks and Keith Rabois are discussed, not speaking in this clip. Lemkin’s descriptions of their preferences are secondhand here.

title: Jason Lemkin: Cold Email Tips; Why Only 15% of Founders Listen to their VCs | 20VC #954
summary: The full interview containing the shorter Lemkin cold-email discussion. Use the linked early segment; most of the episode concerns investing, Algolia and venture capital rather than cold outreach.
notes: Parent interview of nwjEVp8W-co; these are overlapping material, not independent examples.

title: How to Write a Cold Email That Gets a Response
summary: A detailed discussion of credibility, genuine shared connections, useful subject lines, concrete work samples, a precise ask and respecting the recipient’s time. Ferriss describes volunteering with established organizations to create legitimate early credibility.
notes: Includes both cold and connection-based outreach. Names of mutual contacts are not a substitute for an actual relationship.

title: How to write an exceptional cold email.
speakers: Michelle Khare, on Tim Ferriss’s channel
summary: Khare lays out a concise collaboration email: establish legitimacy, explain the proposal and mutual value, show preparation, then make the next step easy.
notes: The speaker is Michelle Khare, not Tim Ferriss. Related to the Ferriss/Khare interview; channel ownership does not identify the speaker.

title: Kevin O'Leary: How To Send A Cold Email
summary: A strong recipient preference for very short messages that say what the sender needs and why. Vague invitations to lunch or an unexplained meeting request do not give him enough reason to engage.
notes: His personal preference and rhetorical response-rate claims should not be treated as measured, universal email rules.

title: Mark Cuban's Cold Email Empire: How $750K Investments Turn Into Billion-Dollar Returns
summary: Cuban recounts investments initiated by email, including the proposal that developed into Cost Plus Drugs. The passage illustrates a compelling business problem and an email exchange that led to deeper investigation.
notes: Edited interview; the Cost Plus Drugs passage also appears in the full episode listed below. It does not reproduce or verify the complete original pitch email.

title: Key Lessons for Every Entrepreneurs, Disrupting the Pharma Industry | Mark Cuban
summary: Full interview containing Cuban’s account of the Cost Plus Drugs cold email and how he expanded the original business idea. The linked segment avoids the rest of the much longer interview.
notes: Same conversation as the edited Cuban episode. Do not count the two uploads as independent corroboration.

title: From Design Agency To $419 Million Holding Company In 8 Years
speakers: Jeremy Giffon / Sam Parr / Shaan Puri
summary: Giffon describes cold outreach as an asymmetric opportunity, while stressing that the sender needs to deliver once the email earns a meeting. Interest and demonstrated ability matter beyond securing a reply.
notes: A firsthand perspective on outreach, not a collection of original email screenshots or a measured response-rate study.

title: Andrew Wilkinson's $20,000 to $260,000,000 story (#521)
speakers: Andrew Wilkinson / Sam Parr / Shaan Puri
summary: Wilkinson recounts emailing Dan Gilbert using a few relevant similarities and a flexible offer to meet. Elsewhere he distinguishes personal networking from acquisition sourcing, where he prefers reputation-driven inbound interest.
notes: The Dan Gilbert exchange is a speaker-reported story; the original email is not independently authenticated here. His acquisition-sourcing preference is not a blanket rejection of all cold email.

title: How a 16-Year-Old Cold Emailed His Way to Alex Hormozi, Noah Kagan, and 500K+ Followers ft. Jay Yang
speakers: Jay Yang, interviewed on No Permission
summary: The sender explains approaching beehiiv with specific project ideas and a pitch deck instead of asking an employer to invent a role. He also describes the preparation behind later creator-work opportunities.
notes: Tyler Denk, Noah Kagan and Alex Hormozi are discussed, not speaking. Yang describes the Noah connection as an introduction through Jeremy Mary; do not label every later role a cold-email outcome.

title: The Unfair Advantage That Gets You Hired
summary: A practical account of reducing hiring friction with concrete project proposals, followed by a cold-outreach framework centered on simple, specific and strategic messages.
notes: Overlaps Yang’s career story in the other interview, but contains a separate presentation of the outreach framework. Employer outcomes are self-reported.

title: He launched a sweaty startup in high school. Now he'll be a millionaire by 18
summary: The hosts coach a young entrepreneur on reaching decision-makers and read or discuss outreach examples, including a student’s message to Elon Musk. They also discuss persistence and leveraging a distinctive personal story.
notes: The hosts’ historical retellings and repeated-follow-up advice are not independently verified here. This contrasts sharply with Ferriss’s more restrained follow-up preference; do not merge them into a universal rule.

title: The Business Ideas Episode: Starting A Better Toastmasters, A SodaStream Competitor & More
summary: The hosts read an email from a listener who had already clipped their podcast content and proposed doing more of the work they wanted. They explain why the concrete work and direct offer earned their attention.
notes: A recipient reaction and hiring-interest story, not proof of a completed job offer or the accuracy of the sender’s projected audience figures.

title: How to Get David Sacks to Open Your Cold Email (Hint: Short & Sweet)
summary: Sacks explains what he needs to see in an inbound SaaS pitch: the business category, stage and meaningful traction. The hosts contrast a concise opportunity summary with long autobiographical introductions.
notes: This is Sacks speaking directly. ARR and growth thresholds reflect his investment context at the time, not requirements for every investor or stage.
